entry.name: Seismoscope
entry.desc: A seismoscope is an instrument that shows that the ground has shaken, without the continuous record that a seismometer keeps. The earliest well-documented one was made in 132 CE by Zhang Heng of the Han dynasty in China and called Houfeng Didong Yi. According to the History of the Later Han Dynasty, it was a bronze vessel about 2 metres across, with eight dragon's heads that dropped a ball into a bronze toad to show the direction of a quake. Mercury and pendulum seismoscopes followed in 18th-century Europe, and the modern seismometer was developed in the 19th century.

row.label: Seismoscope
row.contested: Unverified claims that a device resembling an earthquake detector existed in Ancient Egypt have no confirmation in reliable historical sources. How the central column inside the vessel opened only one dragon's mouth is not known.

notes: The article says Zhang Heng 'is said to have invented the first seismoscope' and calls it 'the earliest well-documented seismoscope': kept as the node. Built on bronze only because the vessel was bronze; drop it if that is too loose.

entry.name: Water clock
entry.desc: A water clock, or clepsydra, measures time by the regulated flow of water into or out of a vessel. Its oldest documentation is the tomb inscription of the 16th-century BCE Egyptian court official Amenemhet, which names him as its inventor, and the oldest surviving one, from the reign of Amenhotep III (c. 1417–1379 BCE), was used at Karnak. Babylonian tablets record water clocks used for the night and day watches, and the oldest written reference in China dates to the 6th century BCE. Ctesibius and other Hellenistic engineers added feedback control, gearing and dials, and water clocks stayed in use until mechanical clocks replaced them in Europe around 1300.

row.label: Water clock
row.contested: The use of water clocks in Babylonian astronomy is traced back to the Old Babylonian Empire (c. 2000–1600 BCE), and N. Narahari Achar and Subhash Kak suggest their use in India as early as the 2nd millennium BCE from the Atharvaveda.

notes: The lead puts the simplest water clocks in Babylon, Egypt and Persia 'around the 16th century BC'; Egypt is the node because it has both the oldest document (Amenemhet) and the oldest physical clock (Karnak, c. 1417-1379 BCE). Year -1550 for 'the 16th century BCE'. Persia's own section says 500 BC, used in also. civ: the Karnak clock is 'in the New Kingdom of Egypt'; Amenemhet's 16th century is the New Kingdom's first century (profile from -1550).

entry.name: Sundial
entry.desc: A sundial tells the time of day from the apparent position of the Sun, usually by the shadow that a gnomon casts on a dial marked with hour-lines. The earliest sundials known from the archaeological record are shadow clocks of about 1500 BCE from ancient Egyptian and Babylonian astronomy. By 240 BCE Eratosthenes had used an obelisk and a water well to estimate the circumference of the world, and the Roman writer Vitruvius listed the dials known in his day in De architectura. Canonical sundials marked the liturgical hours of religious orders from the 7th to the 14th centuries, and Giovanni Padovani published a treatise on making sundials in 1570.

notes: The article gives one sentence on origins: shadow clocks of 1500 BC from Egyptian and Babylonian astronomy, so the place names both and no civ is given (no state is named).

entry.name: Armillary sphere
entry.desc: An armillary sphere is a model of the sky made of rings that stand for the celestial equator, the ecliptic and other circles, centred on the Earth or the Sun. It was invented separately in ancient Greece and in China. Hipparchus credited Eratosthenes (276–194 BCE) with its invention, and Greek armillary spheres served as teaching tools in the 3rd century BCE. In China, Geng Shouchang introduced a fixed equatorial ring in 52 BCE, and Zhang Heng completed the sphere with horizon and meridian rings in 125 CE and turned it by water power. Islamic and medieval European astronomers took it up, and it remained the main instrument for finding celestial positions until the telescope.

row.label: Armillary sphere
row.contested: Joseph Needham traced the Chinese armillary sphere to the single-ring instrument of Shi Shen and Gan De in the 4th century BCE, a dating that Christopher Cullen rejects.

notes: The lead says 'possibly as early as the 4th century BC' for China: that is Needham's dating, rejected by Cullen, so it is in contested and China's also is Cullen's 1st century BCE. Eratosthenes is the inventor only by Hipparchus's attribution (the desc says so).

entry.name: Trigonometry
entry.desc: Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that relates the angles of triangles to the lengths of their sides. It emerged in the Hellenistic world in the 3rd century BCE, when Euclid and Archimedes proved theorems on chords equivalent to later trigonometric formulae, and in 140 BCE Hipparchus gave the first tables of chords. Ptolemy set out detailed tables in his Almagest in the 2nd century CE, and the modern definition of the sine is first attested in the Indian Surya Siddhanta. Persian mathematicians such as Abu al-Wafa used all six trigonometric functions by the 10th century, and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi treated trigonometry as a discipline apart from astronomy.

notes: Dated to Hipparchus's first tables of chords (140 BC), the first trigonometric tables; the field's 3rd-century BCE beginnings with Euclid and Archimedes are in the desc. Could start at -250 instead if the editor prefers the field's emergence. Built on Euclid's Elements (Euclid's chord theorems) and Babylonian astronomy (the Sumerian and Babylonian study of angles and ratios of similar triangles). No also: the Indian sine is a later development of the same field, not an independent origin.

entry.name: Barometer
entry.desc: A barometer is an instrument that measures air pressure, from which changes in the weather can be forecast. Evangelista Torricelli is usually credited with inventing it in 1643, though the historian W. E. Knowles Middleton holds 1644, when Torricelli first reported his experiments, the more likely date. After a water-tube experiment by Gasparo Berti and Raffaello Magiotti, Torricelli argued that the weight of the atmosphere, not the pull of a vacuum, held up the liquid, and he used mercury so that a tube of only 80 cm was needed. In September 1648 Florin Perier carried a barometer up the Puy de Dôme for Blaise Pascal and found that the mercury stood lower at altitude.

row.label: Barometer
row.contested: The 1643 date was suggested only after Torricelli's death. Gasparo Berti built a rudimentary water barometer between 1640 and 1644, and René Descartes described an experiment to measure atmospheric pressure as early as 1631, with no evidence that he built one.

notes: Year 1644 (Middleton's more likely date) rather than the traditional 1643, which is in contested. Place: the article never says where Torricelli worked, only 'Torricelli's gossipy Italian neighborhood' and that Galileo's ideas reached the Rome group; 'Italy' is from 'Italian' (the checker may flag it). No civ: no state is named.

entry.name: Thermometer
entry.desc: A thermometer measures temperature through a change in a sensor that is read against a scale. Philo of Byzantium in the 3rd century BCE and Hero of Alexandria described devices in which heated and cooled air moved water, and in the late 16th and early 17th centuries Galileo Galilei and Santorio Santorio built thermoscopes, which had no scale. The first instrument shown with a scale, and so a thermometer, was Santorio's of 1625; in 1629 Joseph Solomon Delmedigo described a sealed liquid-in-glass thermometer. Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit made a reliable mercury thermometer in 1714, and Anders Celsius proposed his scale in 1742.

row.label: Thermometer
row.contested: Galileo is often said to be the inventor, but no surviving document shows that he made such an instrument. Jean Leurechon described one with a scale of 8 degrees in 1624.

notes: The article says records are sparse and the thermometer is best seen as an evolving technology; dated to Santorio's 1625 drawing, which it calls the first showing a scale. Leurechon's 1624 description of an instrument with an 8-degree scale is a year earlier: put in contested; the editor may prefer 1624. Place 'Italy': Santorio is an 'Italian physiologist' and the article names Padua for him and Delmedigo; Italy is in the article ('late 16th century Italy'). Built on glassmaking for the glass bulb and tube (a plain dependence, not stated).

entry.name: Kite
entry.desc: A kite is a tethered craft heavier than air whose wing surfaces react against the wind to give lift. It was first made in China, where kites of silk and bamboo, and of paper after its invention in the Han dynasty, served to measure distances, test the wind, lift men and signal in war; by 549 CE a kite carried a message for a rescue mission. Kites spread to India, where the fighter kite developed, and across Polynesia, but reached Europe late: Konrad Kyeser described dragon kites about 1400. Benjamin Franklin published an account of a kite experiment on lightning in 1752, and kites served the research of the Wright brothers toward the first airplane.

row.label: Kite
row.contested: The kite has been claimed as the invention of the 5th-century BCE Chinese philosophers Mozi and Lu Ban, who are said to have flown wooden kites called muyuan.

notes: Lane moved from science to transport: the article defines the kite as 'a tethered heavier-than-air craft', tells of man-lifting kites and of kites in the Wright brothers' work on the first airplane; its scientific use comes only in the 18th-19th centuries. Year 549 is the first dated use; the Mozi and Lu Ban origin is only 'claimed', so it is in contested. Paper kites came 'with the invention of paper in the Han dynasty' but undated, so no Han civ. Built on silk (silk sails and lines) and papermaking (paper kites).

entry.name: Lathe
entry.desc: A lathe is a machine tool that turns a workpiece about an axis while tools cut, sand, drill or shape it into a form symmetrical about that axis. Clear evidence of turning comes from the 6th century BCE: fragments of a wooden bowl in an Etruscan tomb in northern Italy and two wooden dishes with turned rims from present-day Turkey. A painting in the tomb of Petosiris in 4th-century BCE Egypt is the first known picture of a lathe, and in China rotary lathes sharpened tools and weapons by about 400 BCE. Andrey Nartov built a lathe with a tool-carrying carriage and gears in 1718, and by the 1770s precision lathes with a slide-rest had become practical.

row.label: Lathe
row.contested: Tenuous evidence of a turned artifact at a Mycenaean Greek site may go back to the 13th or 14th century BCE.

notes: The article contradicts itself: it calls the Petosiris tomb depiction (4th century BC) 'the earliest evidence of a lathe' and then gives 'clear evidence of turned artifacts' from the 6th century BC; the node takes the turned artifacts as the earliest firm evidence. Turkey has turned dishes of the same century, not named as a separate origin. China c. 400 BC (Warring States) in also, since the article does not link it to the Mediterranean. Built on the potter's wheel: the article calls the potter's wheel the best-known lathe design for pottery; drop it if that reads as a kind of lathe rather than a parent.

entry.name: Screw
entry.desc: A screw is a helically threaded fastener tightened or released by twisting its head, and one of the six classical simple machines. It was one of the last simple machines to be invented, first appearing in Mesopotamia in the Neo-Assyrian period (911–609 BCE) and later in Ancient Egypt and Greece, where Archytas of Tarentum described it. By the 1st century BCE wooden screws drove the presses that pressed olive oil and grape juice around the Mediterranean. Metal screws became common fasteners only from the 1760s, when Job and William Wyatt patented a screw machine, and Jesse Ramsden made the first satisfactory screw-cutting lathe in 1777.

notes: The article dates the first screw only to the Neo-Assyrian period (911-609 BC); year -911 is the period's start, circa 1. civ 'Assyrian Empire' is the profile covering the Neo-Assyrian period (to -609). Archytas described it, so he is not listed as inventor. No parent fits (the lathe in this batch is later).

entry.name: Loom
entry.desc: A loom is a device for weaving cloth and tapestry that holds the warp threads under tension while the weft threads are passed over and under them. The earliest evidence of a horizontal loom is a picture on a pottery dish from ancient Egypt dated to 4400 BCE, showing a frame loom with treadles that left the weaver's hands free to pass and beat the weft. The warp-weighted loom, whose warp is kept taut by hanging weights, may go back to the Neolithic. The drawloom for patterned silk is first confirmed by fabrics from the State of Chu of about 400 BCE; it sped up Chinese silk weaving and was introduced to Persia, India and Europe.

row.label: Loom
row.contested: The warp-weighted loom may have originated earlier, in the Neolithic period.

notes: The article's only dated first evidence is the Egyptian pottery dish of 4400 BC (a horizontal frame loom); the warp-weighted loom 'may have originated in the Neolithic' without a date, so it is in contested. No parent: the article does not say what the loom first wove (the cotton and silk nodes are not tied to it).

entry.name: Sewing needle
entry.desc: A sewing needle is a slender pointed tool with an eye at one end to carry thread through material. A needle of bird bone found in Denisova Cave and attributed to the Denisovans is estimated to be about 50,000 years old, and a bone needle from Potok Cave in Slovenia dates to the Aurignacian, 47,000 to 41,000 years ago. Bone and ivory needles come from Xiaogushan in Liaoning and from Kostenki in Russia, and Flinders Petrie found copper sewing needles at Naqada in Egypt dating from 4400 to 3000 BCE. Iron needles are known from the third century BCE, and needle-making began at Redditch in England in 1639.

row.label: Sewing needle
row.contested: Bone awls from Blombos Cave in southern Africa date to 73,000–70,000 years ago, and a point from Sibudu Cave in South Africa, 61,000 years old, might be from a bone needle.

notes: Entry dates left empty: the first needle's date has five digits (it is in the desc and on the card only, as for the stone tools). The Denisova needle is the oldest the article accepts as a needle; the Sibudu point 'might be' one, in contested. No civ: the Denisovans have no profile or entry. Place: the article does not say where Denisova Cave is (Siberia), so it stays bare.

entry.name: Pencil
entry.desc: A pencil is a writing or drawing implement with a solid core of pigment, usually graphite, in a protective casing. Around 1560 the Italian couple Simonio and Lyndiana Bernacotti made what are likely the first plans for a wood-encased pencil, from a hollowed stick of juniper. In 1565 a large deposit of pure, solid graphite, then thought to be a form of lead and called plumbago, was found at Seathwaite in Borrowdale, Cumbria, England, and its sticks were at first wrapped in string or sheepskin. The first attempt to make graphite sticks from powder was in Nuremberg in 1662, and in 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté fired powdered graphite with clay, the method still in use.

row.label: Pencil
row.contested: Some sources date the discovery of the Borrowdale graphite as early as 1500.

notes: Year 1560 (the Bernacottis' plans, 'around 1560'), date '1560s' to cover the Borrowdale graphite of 1565. The article does not date when the graphite was first used for pencils ('the usefulness of graphite for pencils was also discovered'; the meaning 'apparently evolved late in the 16th century'). Place is Borrowdale, where the graphite pencil began; the Bernacottis were Italian (no place given). People are the Bernacottis for the wood-encased design; Conté's clay method (1795, found earlier by Joseph Hardtmuth in 1790) is in the desc only.
